new_statements.quote: Stressed [ə] and [ɤ] occur very rarely, and often in words of probable Shan origin, viz. 'ink, yellow, hundred thousand, crossbow'. Other examples are 'hiccoughs' (onom.?) and 'coffin'. Unstressed [ə̆] is occasionally used by Luce in preference to [ă], but ă is used regularly here. [...] Luce had trouble in pinning down the differences between vowels of adjacent degrees of tongue height, and once again it must be stressed that the transcription is a phonetic one, and pre-phonological at this stage.
new_statements.citation: Henderson, Eugénie J. A. 1986. Some hitherto unpublished material on Northern (Megyaw) Hpun. In John McCoy & Timothy Light (eds.), Contributions to Sino-Tibetan Studies, 101-134. Leiden: E. J. Brill. [Rosetta Project excerpt pp. 106-111]
new_statements.reading: tone language with a stress statement
new_statements.rule_in_words: No source opened states where word stress falls. Henderson's phonetic write-up of Luce's 1962 Megyaw notes treats syllables as stressed or unstressed (unstressed syllables have reduced [ə̆]/[ă], i.e. the sesquisyllabic prefix syllables kə-, tə-, ə- etc. that Taylor and Yabu describe), and her tone analysis, as digested by Namkung 1996 pp. 136-138, has three marks: high level, falling/low level, and 'unstressed syllable (or tone not determined)', with Luce's verdict that Hpun is 'barely tonal, like Tibetan' though minimal pairs exist. The implied pattern is a two-tone system on the main (final) syllable with toneless, unstressed prefix syllables, but that is inference; the section that would state it (pp. 112-114) was not opened.
new_statements.exceptions: Stressed central vowels only in probable Shan loans; some medial sandhi (voicing, nasal, stop insertion) between prefix and main syllable (pp. 108-109).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level phonetic transcription of a c. 820-item elicited wordlist (Luce, October 1962, two elderly Megyaw speakers); phonemic status of tones and stress explicitly left open ('pre-phonological').
new_statements.identity_note: All primary data are the Megyaw (Northern) dialect of Hpun (Luce 1962, two elderly speakers near Sinbo, Myitkyina district); the Samong (Southern) dialect was already extinct by 1962 and is attested only in Taylor 1921 word tables. Glottolog has a single languoid hpon1238 for both; no separate glottocode for Megyaw.

sources.note: Only the Rosetta Project excerpt (pp. 106-111: consonants, glides, syllabic nasals, sandhi, vowels) is open. It is a phonetic, 'pre-phonological' write-up of Luce's 1962 field notes. p. 110 distinguishes stressed and unstressed syllables in the transcription ('Stressed [ə] and [ɤ] occur very rarely... Unstressed [ə̆] is occasionally used by Luce in preference to [ă]') but gives no rule for where stress falls. The tones section (pp. 112-114 per Namkung) is not in the excerpt; full chapter is Brill-paywalled (DOI 10.1163/9789004655409_005) and HathiTrust search-only.

sources.note: Four-page overview in Japanese (dialects, speaker numbers, published wordlists, prefixes, finals -ʔ/-ŋ). Nothing on tone or stress. Names Tun Aung Kyaw 2001 'Hpun sound system' (23 pp., Yangon University, unpublished, in Burmese) and Yabu (ed.) 2003 The Hpun language endangered in Myanmar as the fuller reports.

sources.citation: Namkung, Ju (ed.). 1996. Phonological Inventories of Tibeto-Burman Languages (STEDT Monograph 3). Berkeley: Center for Southeast Asia Studies. 'HPUN (Megyaw/Northern)', pp. 136-138.
sources.note: Second-hand digest of Henderson 1986 pp. 106-114. TONES table: high (or mid-high) level / 'unstressed syllable (or tone not determined)' / falling or low level; note: 'Although Luce set up a two-tone system for Hpun (with basically a high vs. low distinction), he later concluded that the language was "barely tonal, like Tibetan". Nevertheless, there are some minimal pairs.' No placement rule for stress.

sources.citation: Taylor, L. F. 1921. The dialects of Burmese (I). Journal of the Burma Research Society 11(2): 89-97 + comparative tables.
sources.note: Hpon remarks pp. 91-92 (archaic dialect of Burmese, disyllables with ka- prefix, Samong and Megyaw sub-dialects); comparative word tables with Samong Hpon and Megyaw Hpon columns. No statement on Hpun stress; the 'stressed/unstressed syllable' key in the tables describes Burmese tone categories.
